system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2168-12-24 03:20:00 to 2168-12-29 13:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, congestive heart failure, and glaucoma was admitted for acute onset blurry vision in her left eye, which was her better-seeing eye with only 20% visual acuity and severe peripheral vision loss at baseline. Imaging revealed a small chronic brain infarct but no acute stroke, and ophthalmology suspected worsening proliferative diabetic retinopathy as the cause of vision change. She also presented with uncontrolled diabetes, acute kidney injury, and hypovolemia, likely exacerbated by diuretic use. Her diuretics were held, IV fluids were given cautiously, and her kidney function improved. Blood and urine cultures showed no infection. She was stabilized, educated on symptom monitoring, and discharged with plans for ophthalmology follow-up and medication adjustments.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Patient with Charcot deformity with worsening infection
underlying the fifth metatarsal base.  Evaluate for evidence of osteomyelitis.

COMPARISON:  Multiple foot radiographs, most recent ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Right foot, three views.

FINDINGS:  Compared with prior examination, there is little overall change in
the neuropathic joint with extensive sclerosis, heterotopic bone formation and
architectural disintegration.  Vascular calcification is seen along the dorsum
of the right foot.  A plantar ulcer is identified, with a rim of thickened
soft tissue in the base of the fifth metatarsal, but there is no clear
destructive bone lesion at this level to suggest osteomyelitis. However, in
the lateral view, there is indistinctness of the cortical margin of the
inferior aspect of the calcaneous. Calcaneal plantar spurs as well as an os
trigonum are re-identified.

IMPRESSION:  
1.  Indistinctness of the cortical margin of the inferior aspect of the
calcaneous raises concern for osteomyelitis. Further assessment with MR is
recommended. 
2.  No significant change in neuropathic arthropathy of the mid foot and
plantar soft tissue ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in from your podiatrist’s office because of worsening foot ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My left heel and right foot ulcers have been getting worse—more pain, smelly drainage. I’ve been feeling sick all week with vomiting and chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugars have been hard to control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Very hard. I was checking at home and they were over 600. My podiatrist started me on ciprofloxacin, but I didn’t feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your labs show a high white blood cell count, which means your body is fighting an infection. Your kidney function is also temporarily worse, likely from dehydration and the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, my kidneys again? I’ve had that before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an acute on chronic issue. Your baseline kidney function isn’t normal, but this flare-up is likely due to the infection and high sugars. We’ll give IV fluids and treat the infection, and it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about my feet? They hurt so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry saw you in the ER and cleaned out the ulcers. They found a lot of pus and debris. We’re starting IV antibiotics—vancomycin and ciprofloxacin—to cover the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They may need to debride the ulcers again. There was concern on the X-ray about possible bone infection in your heel. We might need an MRI to check that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bone infection? That sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a concern, but not confirmed. The X-ray wasn’t clear. We’ll wait for more info. For now, we’re treating aggressively with antibiotics and wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. And my blood sugar—what are we doing about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started an insulin drip to bring it down safely. The diabetes team will help adjust your long-term insulin plan once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on insulin for years, but it’s getting harder to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, infections and gastroparesis make it harder. We’re continuing your omeprazole and zofran for nausea. We tried reglan, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated too. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ve started lactulose to help. Once you’re eating better, it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have an update. The cultures from your foot ulcers came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh? What did they find?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas and some Group B Strep. Good news—the Pseudomonas is sensitive to the antibiotics you’re on. No MRSA, which we were worried about given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your white count is already coming down. Podiatry took you to the OR yesterday for a more thorough debridement. They didn’t see any obvious bone involvement, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So no osteomyelitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that they could see. We’ll still watch closely. You’ll finish a course of antibiotics at home—doxycycline for MRSA coverage and levofloxacin for the Pseudomonas and Strep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Bactrim—glad we’re not using that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted your allergies. Doxycycline is a safe alternative for MRSA prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be on those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three weeks. You’ll follow up with podiatry, and they’ll decide when to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking better. Creatinine is down to 1.8, which is close to your baseline. Blood sugar is stable on the new insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit better. Still nauseous, but I kept down some toast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re keeping you on omeprazole and zofran. The lactulose helped with bowel movement yesterday, so we’ll keep that as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds? I usually take losartan at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it initially because your potassium was high. It’s coming down now, so we restarted it at a lower dose. We’ll increase it back to 50 mg by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t want my blood pressure to spike.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. White count is normal, no fever, sugars are in the 90s. Podiatry redressed your feet yesterday—negative pressure therapy on the right, wet-to-dry on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I walk at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only for transfers, and only on your left forefoot. Right foot must stay non-weight bearing. You’ll go to rehab for physical therapy and wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rehab? How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days to a week, depending on how quickly you heal and regain strength. They’ll help with mobility and teach you dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs this morning are excellent. Potassium is 4.9, sodium 138, creatinine 1.8. You’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the antibiotics as prescribed. Do saline wet-to-dry dressings daily. Keep the right foot non-weight bearing. Monitor blood sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? It’s different now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Levemir 10 units in the morning, 5 at bedtime, NPH 30 in the morning, and a sliding scale with Humalog. The diabetes team adjusted it for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help remembering that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will go over it with you, and you’ll have written instructions. Also, check your feet daily for any new redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always do. I don’t want to lose a foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing everything right by coming in early. That’s how we prevent worse complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Ready to get out of here, but a bit nervous about managing everything at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. That’s why you’re going to rehab. They’ll support you with meds, wound care, and mobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And podiatry follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about a week. They’ll assess healing and adjust the plan. Also, get your electrolytes checked in a few days due to the losartan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I watch for infection signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Fever, increased redness, swelling, or drainage. If any of those, call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up the good work.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes and multiple complications, including neuropathy, gastroparesis, and chronic foot ulcers, was admitted for worsening bilateral foot infections. She presented with uncontrolled blood sugars, leukocytosis, and acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration and infection. She underwent debridement of both foot ulcers, with negative pressure wound therapy applied to the right foot. Cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Group B Streptococcus, and she was treated with targeted IV antibiotics, later transitioned to oral doxycycline and levofloxacin. Her infection resolved, renal function improved, and blood glucose stabilized on a revised insulin regimen. She was discharged to extended care with wound care instructions, non-weight-bearing status on the right foot, and plans for close podiatry follow-up.
